lede: $\dfrac{12}{18}$ cancels to $\dfrac{2}{3}$ because 6 divides the whole of the top and the whole of the bottom. An algebraic fraction is the same idea with brackets doing the dividing, and the brackets are invisible until you factorise. So factorising is not the first step; it is the only step that makes the others possible.
can: Factorise a numerator and a denominator fully, common factor first.
Cancel a matching bracket, and say why a matching term does not cancel.
Finish the job: check the numbers as well as the brackets.

md: Every algebraic fraction question on this paper begins the same way, and the examiners have said so three years running: **factorise first**. Candidates who do not are reported as tying themselves in knots with cubic tops and bottoms that will not cancel. This is also the skill the next two topics stand on — multiplying, dividing, adding and subtracting all end with a cancel, and the cancel is this.

caption: A matching pair of brackets divides out. A matching pair of terms does not, and one substitution proves it.

prompt: One tap to start. What is $x^{2}-9$ as a product of two brackets?
explain: A difference of two squares: $x^{2}-3^{2}$. It is the single most useful factorisation in this unit, and it is about to do most of the work.

text: Why cancelling works, and when it does not

md:
Cancelling is division. When you cancel a bracket from the top and the bottom, you are dividing both lines by that bracket, and dividing the top and the bottom of a fraction by the same non-zero thing leaves its value alone. That is the whole justification.
It also tells you exactly what may be cancelled: a **factor**, meaning something the whole line is multiplied by. A **term** is added to the rest of the line, so dividing by it does not divide the line, and the value changes.

explain: The $x$ on top is a term, not a factor. Substituting $x = 1$ gives $5$ for the fraction and $4$ for the cancelled version, so they are different expressions.

md: **1 Factorise the numerator fully.** Common factor first, then the quadratic. Taking the number out first is often what makes the rest visible: $4x^{2}-100$ looks unpromising until the 4 comes out and leaves a difference of two squares.

prompt: A numerator is $x^{3}-9x$. What is the first line you write?
options: It is a cubic, so it does not factorise
explain: Take the common factor $x$ out first. What is left is a difference of two squares, so the full factorisation is $x(x-3)(x+3)$. Every cubic on this paper factorises this way.

md:
**2 Factorise the denominator fully**, the same way.
**3 Cancel every factor that appears on both lines**, and then look at the numbers. That last look is where the marks go.

explain: $4x^{2}-25$ is $(2x)^{2}-5^{2}$. The square root of $4x^{2}$ is $2x$: that is the step candidates miss when a coefficient is involved.

title: Simplifying Algebraic Fractions
why: The full method at writing speed, with several of the shapes CCEA uses. Watch it once, then answer the gate below without scrolling back.

explain: Top $(x+5)(x+2)$, bottom $(x+5)(x-2)$, and $(x+5)$ divides out. The second option is that same line before any cancelling; the third strikes out the two $x^{2}$ terms, which are terms of a sum.

md:
The word **fully** is doing real work in the instruction. It means there is nothing left that divides both lines — no bracket and no number.
Two shapes catch people: a number left over, such as a 2 on top and a 4 underneath, and an $x$ left over when both lines still carry one.

title: Summer 2024, FM1 Q8(a)
md: Nearly everyone factorised and cancelled correctly, and then stopped one step early: a factor of 2 was left standing in the answer. The algebra was right and the final mark went with it.

explain: The 6 and the 3 share a factor of 3. Multiplying the bracket out, as the third option does, is not simplifying: it hides the factors and changes nothing.

title: Why the last look at the numbers matters
md: Cancelling a bracket and cancelling a number are the same operation: dividing the whole top and the whole bottom by something. A 2 over a 4 is as much a common factor as a bracket is, so an answer is only fully simplified when neither is left.

prompt: Erin has reached $\frac{3x^{2}}{x}$. Is that her answer?
options: No — an $x$ divides both lines, giving $3x$
answer: No — an $x$ divides both lines, giving $3x$
explain: Both lines still carry an $x$ as a factor, so it divides out and leaves $3x$. This is the shape the Summer 2023 report picked out by name.

md:
Factorise both lines fully, common factor first.
Cancel matching brackets, never matching terms.
Check the numbers before you call it finished.

The wording is **Simplify fully**, three or four marks, and on recent papers it has sat around Q7 to Q10. A mark comes for each line factorised and one for the cancelled answer. The first mark is a factorisation, so factorise even when you cannot see where the question is going. The last mark is the word fully. Stuck: if a numerator is a cubic, take the common factor out before anything else.
